title: The Artifact ships a pre-written wind-down sequence that ends by repaying Spark's USDS debt
content:
A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.2.2.3 contains a complete capital retreat, written as executable one-liners. On L2s: `foreignController.redeemERC4626(address(token), token.balanceOf(address(proxy)))`, `foreignController.withdrawAave(aToken, aToken.balanceOf(address(proxy)))`, and `foreignController.withdrawPSM(address(usdc), type(uint256).max)` — each using the full balance rather than a specified amount. Then `foreignController.transferUSDCToCCTP(usdc.balanceOf(address(proxy)), 0)` to bring everything to Mainnet (domain 0). Then on Mainnet the same full-balance redemptions, followed by `mainnetController.swapUSDCToUSDS(...)` and finally `mainnetController.burnUSDS(usds.balanceOf(address(proxy)))` to "repay and then burn Spark's USDS debt."

The sequence has a clear shape: pull positions back to each chain's ALM Proxy, consolidate to Mainnet, convert everything to USDS, extinguish the debt. Its endpoint is not "funds are safe" but "the liability to Sky is gone" — which is the correct terminal state given that Spark's capital is drawn against a Sky Allocation Vault.

Writing it in advance is the substantive contribution. In a crisis the scarce resource is decision-making, and "withdraw everything" is a deceptively large number of correctly ordered calls across seven chains and a dozen venues. Pre-authoring them removes both the sequencing risk and the argument about what to do first.

It also depends on choices made elsewhere: outflow rate limits set to Unlimited and rate limits that credit on reversal are what make a full-balance exit executable in one pass. The emergency path was designed backwards from the limits, not bolted on.
description: Emergency actions redeem every ERC-4626 and Aave position at full balance, drain the PSM with type(uint256).max, bridge USDC to domain 0, swap to USDS and burn it
